obligations.title: Notifiable Data Breaches: assess a suspected eligible data breach
obligations.rule: An entity that is aware of reasonable grounds to suspect an eligible data breach, and is not yet aware of reasonable grounds to believe that one has occurred, must carry out a reasonable and expeditious assessment. It must take all reasonable steps to complete that assessment within 30 days after it becomes aware of the suspicion. The Act frames the 30 days as the period for those reasonable steps, not as a hard stop.
obligations.quote: take all reasonable steps to ensure that the assessment is completed within 30 days after the entity becomes aware as mentioned in paragraph (1)(a).

verification.note: Quote and deadline checked against the source text on 2026-11-28.

obligations.recipient: No external recipient. This is an internal assessment duty.

clocks.name: assessment
clocks.basis: All reasonable steps to complete the assessment within 30 days after awareness (Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) s 26WH(2)).

obligations.title: Notifiable Data Breaches: statement to the Commissioner and notice to individuals
obligations.rule: Once the entity is aware of reasonable grounds to believe there has been an eligible data breach, it must prepare a statement and give a copy to the Commissioner as soon as practicable. It must notify the individuals to whom the information relates, or if that is not practicable the individuals at risk, as soon as practicable after the statement is prepared. If neither is practicable, it must publish the statement and take reasonable steps to publicise it. Section 26WL(3) requires compliance with the notification duty as soon as practicable after the preparation of the statement is completed.
obligations.quote: do so as soon as practicable after the entity becomes so aware.

verification.note: Quote and deadline checked against the source text on 2026-11-28.

obligations.recipient: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (statement), then the individuals concerned or at risk (notice).
obligations.channel: The OAIC notifiable data breach form, then notice to individuals. A person lodges and sends them.

obligations.title: SOCI Act: critical cyber security incident report
obligations.citation: Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018 (Cth) s 30BC
obligations.rule: A responsible entity for a critical infrastructure asset that becomes aware a cyber security incident has occurred or is occurring, and that the incident has had or is having a significant impact on the availability of the asset, must give the relevant Commonwealth body a report as soon as practicable and within 12 hours. Section 30BEA says a significant impact requires material disruption to the availability of essential goods or services the asset is used to provide, unless the rules specify another circumstance. The report may be oral or in writing. If it is oral, a written record in the approved form is due within 84 hours after the oral report.
obligations.quote: do so as soon as practicable, and in any event within 12 hours, after the entity becomes so aware.

verification.note: Quote and deadline checked against the source text on 2026-11-28.

obligations.recipient: The relevant Commonwealth body under SOCI Act s 30BF. That is ASD's ACSC unless rules name another body.
obligations.channel: ASD reporting page or the Australian Cyber Security Hotline 1300 CYBER1 (1300 292 371). A person reports.

clocks.name: notification
clocks.basis: As soon as practicable, and in any event within 12 hours after awareness (SOCI Act 2018 (Cth) s 30BC).

clocks.name: written_record
clocks.basis: If the report is oral, within 84 hours after the oral report is given. This clock does not start at awareness (SOCI Act 2018 (Cth) s 30BC(3)).

obligations.title: SOCI Act: other cyber security incident report
obligations.citation: Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018 (Cth) s 30BD
obligations.rule: A responsible entity that becomes aware a cyber security incident has occurred, is occurring or is imminent, and that it has had, is having or is likely to have a relevant impact on the asset, must report within 72 hours. Section 30BD does not exempt an incident that section 30BC also covers, so the earlier 12 hour clock is the one to meet when both apply. Section 8G treats a relevant impact as an impact on availability, integrity, reliability or confidentiality. The report may be oral or in writing. If it is oral, a written record is due within 48 hours after the oral report.
obligations.quote: do so as soon as practicable, and in any event within 72 hours, after the entity becomes so aware.

verification.note: Quote and deadline checked against the source text on 2026-11-28.

obligations.recipient: The relevant Commonwealth body under SOCI Act s 30BF. That is ASD's ACSC unless rules name another body.
obligations.channel: ASD reporting page or the Australian Cyber Security Hotline 1300 CYBER1 (1300 292 371). A person reports.

clocks.name: notification
clocks.basis: As soon as practicable, and in any event within 72 hours after awareness (SOCI Act 2018 (Cth) s 30BD).

clocks.name: written_record
clocks.basis: If the report is oral, within 48 hours after the oral report is given. This clock does not start at awareness (SOCI Act 2018 (Cth) s 30BD(3)).

obligations.title: Ransomware payment report
obligations.rule: A reporting business entity that makes a ransomware payment, or becomes aware that another entity provided one on its behalf, must give the designated Commonwealth body a ransomware payment report within 72 hours of the payment or of that awareness, whichever applies. Section 26(2) defines a reporting business entity as a business carried on in Australia whose turnover for the previous financial year is above the threshold prescribed by the rules, excluding Commonwealth bodies, State bodies and responsible entities for critical infrastructure assets, or as a responsible entity for a critical infrastructure asset to which SOCI Act Part 2B applies. Section 8 says that if the rules do not name another body, the designated Commonwealth body is the Department and ASD. The report must be in the form approved by the Secretary and in the manner prescribed by the rules. The Cyber Security (Ransomware Payment Reporting) Rules 2025 s 6 set the turnover threshold at AUD 3 million (pro rata for a business carried on for only part of the year). The Act says turnover must exceed the threshold; the ASD form says equal to or exceeds. Get advice if turnover is close to AUD 3 million.
obligations.quote: The reporting business entity must give the designated Commonwealth body a report (a ransomware payment report) that complies with the requirements of this section within 72 hours of making the ransomware payment or becoming aware that the ransomware payment has been made (whichever is applicable).

obligations.title: APRA CPS 234: material information security incident
obligations.citation: Prudential Standard CPS 234 Information Security, paragraph 35
obligations.rule: An APRA-regulated entity must notify APRA as soon as possible, and no later than 72 hours, after becoming aware of an information security incident that materially affected, or had the potential to materially affect, financially or non-financially, the entity or the interests of depositors, policyholders, beneficiaries or other customers, or that has been notified to other regulators in Australia or other jurisdictions. A statement to the OAIC under the NDB scheme is a notification to another regulator.

obligations.title: APRA CPS 234: material control weakness that cannot be fixed in time

obligations.title: Voluntary report to ASD's ACSC (ReportCyber)
obligations.citation: ASD, Report a cyber security incident
obligations.rule: Any organisation can report a cyber security incident to ASD's ACSC. ASD asks for a report as soon as possible after becoming aware of an incident. This is guidance, not a statutory duty, and it does not replace any mandatory report.

obligations.title: Voluntary information to the National Cyber Security Coordinator (significant incident)
obligations.rule: If an incident is, or could reasonably be expected to be, a significant cyber security incident (s 34), the impacted entity may give information about it to the National Cyber Security Coordinator at any time during the response (s 35). There is no obligation to do so. Section 38 limits how the Coordinator may record, use or disclose that information, including a bar on using it to investigate or enforce most contraventions by the entity. Section 44 says giving information under this Part does not affect any other requirement to provide it, such as a SOCI Part 2B report or a ransomware payment report.
obligations.quote: Information provided by an entity under this Part does not affect any other requirement of the entity to provide that information under this Act or another law of the Commonwealth.

verification.note: Quote and deadline checked against the source text on 2026-11-28.

obligations.channel: Through the Coordinator's office or ASD. A person decides whether to share.

clocks.name: share
clocks.basis: At any time during the response to the incident (Cyber Security Act 2024 s 35(3)). Voluntary.

all.label: the incident is, or could reasonably be expected to be, a significant cyber security incident (s 34)

obligations.not_applicable_note: If the incident could seriously prejudice Australia's social or economic stability, defence or national security, or is of serious concern to the Australian people (s 34), the organisation may share information with the National Cyber Security Coordinator under s 35.

obligations.title: Limited use of information in a ransomware payment report
obligations.rule: Information in a ransomware payment report may be recorded, used or disclosed only for the permitted purposes in s 29(1). The designated Commonwealth body must not use it to investigate or enforce a contravention by the entity of a Commonwealth, State or Territory law, other than Part 3 itself or a criminal offence (s 29(2)). Secondary recipients are bound the same way (s 30). Giving the report does not otherwise affect a claim of legal professional privilege (s 31). The report is generally not admissible in evidence against the entity (s 32). These limits do not cover information already given to meet SOCI Part 2B or the Telecommunications Act, or information already lawfully public (s 29(4)).

obligations.title: ASD's limited use obligation for voluntarily shared information
obligations.citation: Intelligence Services Act 2001 (Cth) Part 6 Division 1A, as described by ASD
obligations.rule: Information an organisation voluntarily gives ASD about a cyber security incident cannot be used by ASD for regulatory purposes, and ASD staff cannot be compelled to give it in most proceedings. The protection does not expire, but it stops applying to information the organisation makes lawfully public. It does not satisfy any mandatory reporting obligation, and it does not stop regulators or police using their own powers to obtain information.
obligations.quote: ASD is not a regulator and providing information under limited use does not acquit your regulatory reporting responsibilities.

verification.note: Checked against ASD's limited use guidance page on 2026-11-28. The Intelligence Services Act 2001 Division 1A text was not fetched for this review, so the section numbers are not quoted here.
